It is the one place the server's settings live. Deploy.ps1 reads it, never overwrites it, and
preserves it across every upgrade - so an edit here survives the next deployment.
After changing anything in this file:   Restart-Service Swarnakshi
This template is committed. The copy on the server holds real passwords and is git-ignored;
do not commit it, and do not copy it back into the repository.
PostgreSQL. This is the only place the application learns where its database is, so a move
to a cloud-hosted server is this one line and a restart.
Host          - machine running PostgreSQL. 'localhost' is this machine; for a cloud server,
its hostname, e.g. mydb.abc123.ap-south-1.rds.amazonaws.com
Port          - 5432 unless the server says otherwise.
Database      - the database name, lower-case, as created by 01-create-database.sql.
Username      - the application role, which OWNS the database (again, 01-create-database.sql).
Password      - that role's password. Change it here and restart the API.
SSL Mode      - add  ;SSL Mode=Require  for any server that is not on this machine. Cloud
providers insist on it, and traffic across a network without it is readable.
Timezone      - leave it out. Every timestamp the application writes is UTC.

//Database: StartupWaitSeconds - how long to keep trying to reach SQL Server before giving up at startup.
On a reboot IIS starts this app as soon as it can, which can be before SQL Server Express is
accepting connections. Failing on the first refusal turns a few seconds of boot ordering into
an outage that lasts until somebody restarts IIS - a process that has died cannot notice the
database arriving a moment later. 60 seconds costs a healthy server nothing and a genuinely
misconfigured one one minute, after which it still fails, just as loudly. Raise it on a slow
machine; it must stay below the app pool's startupTimeLimit, which defaults to 120.

//: Key signs every access and refresh token. It must be at least 32 characters, and the app
refuses to start without it. Generate one once and then LEAVE IT ALONE - changing it signs
every user out. To generate one:
powershell -c "$b=New-Object byte[] 48;(New-Object Security.Cryptography.RNGCryptoServiceProvider).GetBytes($b);[Convert]::ToBase64String($b)"

//Urls: The address and port Kestrel listens on. Behind a Cloudflare tunnel this stays on
localhost: cloudflared runs on this machine and connects out, so nothing needs to reach
the port from the network and no firewall rule is wanted. Bind 0.0.0.0 only if some other
machine on the LAN must reach the service directly.

//: Seed credentials for the EnterpriseAdmin operator account, used ONLY when that row does not
exist yet. Changing the password here after the first run does nothing - change it in the app.
Delete this whole section to keep the application's built-in default.

//Cors: The UI is served by this same process, so a browser on the site's own hostname makes only
same-origin calls and needs nothing here. List an origin when a browser on ANOTHER hostname
must call this API - which is what a separate api. name is for.
//Seed: Demo data is Development-only and is ignored in Production whatever this says.
//Storage: Where uploaded attachments are written. Back this folder up along with the database.
//Logging: Directory - where the rolling log files go. Left out, it defaults to a 'logs' folder beside
the app folder. Outside the app folder on purpose: a deployment replaces that folder, and the
logs explaining why the last one went wrong should outlive it.
One file per day, fourteen kept, 50 MB each at most.
Every failure is written with a short reference that also goes back to the caller, so someone
reporting 'it said error 4f3a9c' is answered by searching the file for that string.
The account the app runs as must be able to write here - under IIS that is the app pool.
